topics.label: Fork, clone, and the core loop

entries.title: git vs GitHub, and what a repository is
entries.summary: git is the version-control program on your computer that records snapshots (commits) of a project folder; GitHub is a website that hosts git repositories so people can share them. A repository is just a folder that git is tracking.
entries.syntax:
git      → the tool, runs on your machine
GitHub   → the website that hosts repositories online
repo     → a project folder tracked by git
fork     → your own copy of someone's repo on GitHub
clone    → a download of a repo onto your machine
commit   → a saved snapshot with a message
entries.gotcha: You can use git without GitHub (snapshots stay on your machine). You cannot use GitHub without git.

entries.title: Do I have git? git --version
entries.summary: Prints the installed version; if the terminal instead says the command is not found, install git from git-scm.com.
entries.syntax: git --version
entries.gotcha: On a Mac, typing `git` for the first time may offer to install the Xcode command-line tools; accept it.

entries.title: git config — tell git who you are
entries.summary: Stores your name and email once, so every commit you make is labelled with them.
entries.syntax:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@email.com"
entries.example:
git config --global user.name "Student Example"
git config --global user.email "student@example.com"
git config --global --list
entries.gotcha: Use the email attached to your GitHub account, or GitHub will not link the commits to you.

entries.title: Personal access token (GitHub)
entries.summary: GitHub does not accept your account password on the command line; a personal access token (PAT) is the password you paste when `git push` asks for one.
entries.syntax:
GitHub → Settings (top-right avatar) → Developer settings → Personal access tokens
       → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token → copy it somewhere safe
entries.gotcha: GitHub shows the token only once. When git asks for a password, paste the token, not your GitHub password.

entries.title: git init — start tracking a folder
entries.summary: Turns the current folder into a Git repository by creating a hidden `.git` folder where every snapshot will be stored. Run it once per project, inside the project folder, before the first commit.
entries.syntax:
cd path/to/project
git init
entries.example:
mkdir minigpt
cd minigpt
git init
ls -a
git status
entries.output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/student/hudm5001/minigpt/.git/
.
..
.git
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
lines: mkdir minigpt
Makes the project folder. Keep the name short, lowercase, no spaces.
cd minigpt
Moves into it. `git init` always acts on the folder you are in.
git init
Creates the hidden `.git` folder and nothing else. Your files are not tracked until you `git add` them.
ls -a
`-a` lists hidden entries too, so you can see that `.git` now exists.
git status
Confirms the branch name (`main`) and that there are no commits yet.
entries.gotcha: Run it in the project folder, never in your home folder: a repository that contains your whole home directory tracks everything you own. If `git status` in a fresh folder already reports a branch, you are inside another repository.

entries.title: .gitignore — files Git must never track
entries.summary: A plain text file named `.gitignore` in the project root. Each line is a pattern; matching files never appear in `git status` and cannot be added by accident. Write it before the first commit, because a file that is committed once stays in the history forever.
entries.syntax:
data/           # a whole folder (trailing slash)
*.pt            # every file with this extension
__pycache__/
.DS_Store
entries.example:
mkdir demo && cd demo && git init -q
printf 'data/\n__pycache__/\n.DS_Store\n' > .gitignore
mkdir data && echo "passenger,age" > data/big.csv
echo "print('hi')" > analysis.py
git status --short
git add .gitignore analysis.py
git commit -q -m "First commit, without the data"
git ls-files
lines: printf '...' > .gitignore
Writes three lines into the file (`\n` is a line break). In real life you would type them in VS Code; the effect is the same.
mkdir data && echo ... > data/big.csv
Creates something that looks like a dataset inside the ignored folder.
git status --short
Lists changes in a compact form: `??` means untracked. `data/` is missing from the list because it is ignored.
git ls-files
Shows what the repository actually tracks: the ignore file and the script, no data.
entries.gotcha: Ignoring a file that is already committed changes nothing; run `git rm --cached path` first, then commit. A folder pattern needs the trailing slash (`data/`), otherwise it also matches a file named `data`.

entries.title: Create an empty repository on GitHub
entries.summary: Your local repository needs a home on GitHub before you can push. Create the GitHub side completely empty, then connect the two with the commands GitHub shows you afterwards. Two ways: click through the website (below), or one command with the GitHub CLI (see `git/gh-repo-create`).
entries.example:
github.com → "+" (top right) → New repository
  Repository name:  minigpt           ← same name as your folder
  Visibility:       Public or Private
  Leave UNTICKED:   Add a README, Add .gitignore, Choose a license
→ Create repository
entries.output_note: GitHub then shows a page with a box titled “…or push an existing repository from the command line”. Its three commands are the next entry.
lines: Repository name
Use the folder name so the URL and the folder match; GitHub URLs are `github.com/<user>/<name>`.
Leave the three boxes unticked
You already have a README and a .gitignore locally. Ticking a box makes GitHub create a first commit that your computer does not have, and your first push is rejected.
Create repository
Nothing is uploaded yet. The repository is an empty shell waiting for `git push`.
entries.gotcha: If you did tick “Add a README”, either delete the repository and recreate it, or run `git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories` once before pushing.

entries.title: gh repo create — make the GitHub repository from the terminal
entries.summary: The GitHub CLI, `gh`, does what the website does, from the terminal: log in once, then create repositories, open pull requests and more without leaving the shell. It also removes the password problem: `gh auth login` stores a token that git uses automatically for every push and pull.
entries.syntax:
conda install -c conda-forge gh      # one time; on a Mac `brew install gh` also works
gh auth login                        # one time per computer
gh repo create <name> --private      # or --public: an EMPTY repository on GitHub
gh repo view <name> --web            # open it in the browser to check
entries.example:
gh auth login
#   ? Where do you use GitHub?            GitHub.com
#   ? Preferred protocol for Git operations?   HTTPS
#   ? Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?   Yes
#   ? How would you like to authenticate?  Login with a web browser
#   (copy the one-time code, press Enter, paste it on the GitHub page that opens)

gh repo create minigpt --private
gh repo view minigpt --web
entries.output_note: Not run here because it needs your GitHub account. After `gh auth login` you see “✓ Logged in as <your-username>”; after `gh repo create` a line with the new repository's address, `https://github.com/<your-username>/minigpt`; `gh repo view --web` opens that page in the browser. The repository is empty, exactly as if you had clicked New repository and left every box unticked.
lines: conda install -c conda-forge gh
Installs the GitHub CLI into the active conda environment. `gh` is a separate program from `git`; installing it does not install or change git.
gh auth login

A one-time login per computer. It asks four questions (answer as shown in the comments), shows a one-time code, opens GitHub in your browser, and you paste the code there. From then on `gh` and `git` share the stored token, so `git push` never asks for a password.
gh repo create minigpt --private

Creates an empty repository named `minigpt` under your account. `--private` or `--public` is required in this non-interactive form; without a name and a flag, `gh repo create` asks questions instead. Nothing is uploaded and no README is added, so the next step (`git remote add origin` … `git push -u origin main`) is the same as after the website route.
gh repo view minigpt --web
Opens the repository page in the browser: the quickest way to confirm it exists and to copy its URL.
gh repo create minigpt --private --source=. --remote=origin --push

The all-in-one form, for later: run inside an existing local repository, it creates the GitHub repository, adds it as `origin`, and pushes your commits, doing the create step and the connect step together.
entries.gotcha: `gh repo create` only makes the GitHub side. Your folder still needs `git init` and a commit before anything can be pushed. If it answers “Name already exists on this account”, you already have a repository called that; pick another name or delete the old one on GitHub.
entries.source: GitHub CLI manual (cli.github.com), `gh repo create --help`, gh 2.100

entries.title: git remote add origin + git push -u — connect and first push
entries.summary: Three commands, the same ones GitHub prints after you create the empty repository: tell Git where the remote lives, make sure the branch is called `main`, and push while remembering the link so that later pushes are just `git push`.
entries.syntax:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/<repo>.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
entries.setup:
mkdir minigpt && cd minigpt && git init -q
echo "# miniGPT" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initialise repository"
# verification only: a local folder stands in for GitHub, and git is told to send
# https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/... there instead of over the network
git init -q --bare "$HOME/github/minigpt.git"
git config --global url."$HOME/github/".insteadOf "https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/"
entries.setup_note: a repository with one commit, plus a local folder standing in for GitHub
entries.example:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/minigpt.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
git remote -v
entries.output:
To /Users/student/github/minigpt.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
origin	/Users/student/github/minigpt.git (fetch)
origin	/Users/student/github/minigpt.git (push)
entries.output_note: On your machine the address is your GitHub URL. Here a local folder stands in for GitHub, so the output names that folder instead.
lines: git remote add origin <URL>
`origin` is the conventional nickname for your GitHub copy. The URL comes from the green **Code** button on GitHub (HTTPS tab).
git branch -M main
Renames the current branch to `main`; older Git versions start on `master`. `-M` renames even if `main` already exists.
git push -u origin main
Uploads your commits. `-u` records that local `main` follows `origin/main`, so plain `git push` and `git pull` work from now on.
git remote -v
Lists the remotes with their addresses, once for fetch and once for push, so you can check the link.
gh repo create minigpt --private --source=. --remote=origin --push
The GitHub CLI shortcut: creates the repository, adds `origin` and pushes in one command, replacing all three lines above. `git remote -v` afterwards shows the same result.
entries.gotcha: GitHub does not accept your account password over HTTPS. When asked for a password, paste a personal access token (see the token entry) or sign in once through GitHub Desktop or the `gh` command-line tool.

entries.title: git switch -c — work on a branch
entries.summary: A branch is a separate line of commits. Create one for an experiment or a feature, commit on it freely, and merge it into `main` only when it works. `git switch` moves between branches; your files change to match.
entries.syntax:
git switch -c experiment/wider-model   # create a branch and move to it
git switch main                        # go back
git branch                             # list branches; * marks the current one
entries.setup:
mkdir minigpt && cd minigpt && git init -q
echo "# miniGPT" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initialise repository"
# verification only: a local folder stands in for GitHub, and git is told to send
# https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/... there instead of over the network
git init -q --bare "$HOME/github/minigpt.git"
git config --global url."$HOME/github/".insteadOf "https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/"
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/minigpt.git && git push -q -u origin main
entries.setup_note: a repository already connected to (a stand-in for) GitHub
entries.example:
git switch -c experiment/wider-model
echo "n_embd: 512" > config.yaml
git add config.yaml
git commit -m "Try a wider model"
git branch
git push -u origin experiment/wider-model
git switch main
ls
entries.output:
Switched to a new branch 'experiment/wider-model'
[experiment/wider-model 0193114] Try a wider model
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 config.yaml
* experiment/wider-model
  main
To /Users/student/github/minigpt.git
 * [new branch]      experiment/wider-model -> experiment/wider-model
branch 'experiment/wider-model' set up to track 'origin/experiment/wider-model'.
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
README.md
lines: git switch -c experiment/wider-model
`-c` creates the branch and switches to it in one step. Slashes in the name are just a naming convention (`experiment/…`, `fix/…`).
echo ... > config.yaml, git add, git commit
Normal work. The commit lands on the new branch; `main` does not change.
git branch
Lists both branches; the `*` shows where you are.
git push -u origin experiment/wider-model
Publishes the branch to GitHub under the same name, which is what a pull request needs.
git switch main / ls
Back on `main` the file `config.yaml` is gone: it exists only on the branch until you merge.
entries.gotcha: Commit before you switch. Uncommitted changes travel with you to the other branch and the two lines of work get mixed up. `git checkout -b` is the older spelling of `git switch -c`; both work.

entries.title: Pull request — propose merging a branch
entries.summary: After you push a branch, GitHub offers to open a pull request: a page that shows the diff, lets teammates comment and approve, and ends with a **Merge** button that folds the branch into `main`. In a solo project it is still worth using, because it is where you write down what the change achieved.
entries.example:
GitHub → your repository → "Compare & pull request" (banner shown after a push)
  base: main   ←   compare: experiment/wider-model
  Title:        Widen the model to n_embd=512
  Description:  what changed, and the number it bought (val loss 1.47, was 1.51)
→ Create pull request → (review) → Merge pull request → Delete branch

Then, on your computer:
git switch main
git pull
git branch -d experiment/wider-model
entries.output_note: Nothing runs locally until the last three commands; they bring the merged result down and delete the finished branch.
lines: base ← compare
`base` is where the change goes (`main`); `compare` is the branch that holds it.
Description
Put the result in words and numbers. Six weeks later this text, not your memory, is what a report is written from.
Merge pull request
GitHub creates a merge commit on `main`. Your laptop does not know yet.
git switch main + git pull
Downloads the merged commits so local `main` matches GitHub.
git branch -d …
`-d` deletes the local branch only if it has been merged, so it is safe.
entries.gotcha: If GitHub says the branch has conflicts, `main` moved while you worked. Run `git pull origin main` on your branch, fix the marked files, commit, push again, and the button turns green.

entries.title: Fork — your own copy on GitHub
entries.summary: Forking copies someone else's repository into your GitHub account, where you are free to change it.
entries.syntax:
open https://github.com/cgpan/hudm5001  →  click Fork (top right)
→ you now own https://github.com/<your-username>/hudm5001
entries.gotcha: Fork on the website first, then clone your fork, not the original. Pushing to the original course repo is not allowed.

entries.title: git clone — download a repo
entries.summary: Copies a repository from GitHub (or any location) onto your machine, into a new folder with the repo's name.
entries.syntax:
cd path/to/where/you/keep/projects
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/hudm5001.git
cd hudm5001
entries.setup:
cd ~
git init -q --bare course-repo.git
git clone -q course-repo.git seed 2>/dev/null && cd seed
echo "# HUDM 5001 course materials" > README.md
git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initial commit" && git push -q origin main
cd ~ && rm -rf seed
entries.setup_note: a small course repo to clone from (standing in for GitHub)
entries.example:
cd ~
git clone course-repo.git hudm5001-demo
cd hudm5001-demo
ls
entries.gotcha: The URL comes from the green Code button on the repo page. Clone once; after that use `git pull` to get updates, never clone again into the same folder.

entries.title: git status — what changed?
entries.summary: Shows which files are new (untracked), modified, or staged for the next commit. Run it before and after every other git command.
entries.syntax: git status
entries.setup:
git init -q hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
entries.setup_note: a fresh repo with one new file
entries.output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	assignment1.py

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
entries.gotcha: “Untracked” means git has never seen the file; it is not saved anywhere until you `add` and `commit` it.

entries.title: git add — stage a file
entries.summary: Marks a file to be included in the next snapshot; `git add .` stages everything in the folder. Think: put items in the box.
entries.syntax:
git add file
git add .
entries.setup:
git init -q hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
entries.setup_note: a fresh repo with one new file
entries.output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   assignment1.py
entries.gotcha: Staging is not saving. Nothing is recorded until `git commit`.

entries.title: git commit -m — save a snapshot
entries.summary: Records the staged files as a snapshot with a message saying what you did and why. Think: seal and label the box.
entries.syntax: git commit -m "short message"
entries.setup:
git init -q hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
git add assignment1.py
entries.setup_note: a fresh repo with one staged file
entries.output:
[main (root-commit) ddee85a] Finish assignment 1
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 assignment1.py
entries.output_note: The 7-character code is the commit's id; every commit gets a different one.
entries.gotcha: The message must be in quotes. Forget `-m` and git opens a text editor waiting for a message.

entries.title: git push — upload your commits
entries.summary: Sends your committed snapshots up to your GitHub fork. Think: mail the box. The first push asks for your username and personal access token.
entries.syntax: git push
entries.setup:
cd ~ && git init -q --bare course-repo.git
git clone -q course-repo.git seed 2>/dev/null && cd seed && echo "# HUDM 5001" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initial commit" && git push -q origin main && cd ~ && rm -rf seed
git clone -q course-repo.git hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
git add assignment1.py && git commit -q -m "Finish assignment 1"
entries.setup_note: a clone of the course repo with one new commit not yet uploaded
entries.gotcha: Push only after `commit`; there is nothing to push otherwise (“Everything up-to-date”). Never paste your token into a shared notebook.

entries.title: git log --oneline — view history
entries.summary: Lists commits, newest first, one per line with the short id and the message.
entries.syntax:
git log --oneline
git log --oneline -5    # only the last 5
entries.setup:
git init -q hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
git add assignment1.py && git commit -q -m "Finish assignment 1"
echo "# notes" > README.md
git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Add README"
entries.output:
d7b6e5f Add README
ddee85a Finish assignment 1
entries.gotcha: Press `q` to leave the log view if it opens in a pager.

entries.title: git diff — what exactly changed
entries.summary: Shows the line-by-line difference between your edited files and the last commit; `-` lines were removed, `+` lines were added.
entries.syntax:
git diff
git diff file
entries.setup:
git init -q hudm5001-demo && cd hudm5001-demo
echo "print('assignment 1')" > assignment1.py
git add assignment1.py && git commit -q -m "Finish assignment 1"
echo "print('assignment 1, revised')" > assignment1.py
entries.setup_note: a committed file that has since been edited
entries.output:
diff --git a/assignment1.py b/assignment1.py
index 12502de..5e030fd 100644
--- a/assignment1.py
+++ b/assignment1.py
@@ -1 +1 @@
-print('assignment 1')
+print('assignment 1, revised')
entries.gotcha: `git diff` shows unstaged edits only. After `git add`, use `git diff --staged` to see what is about to be committed.

entries.title: Sync fork — update your GitHub copy
entries.summary: When the instructor adds material to the original repo, the website can copy those commits into your fork with two clicks.
entries.syntax: open your fork on GitHub  →  “Sync fork” dropdown  →  “Update branch”
entries.gotcha: This updates the copy on GitHub only. Follow it with `git pull` on your machine to bring the files down.

entries.title: git pull — download the latest commits
entries.summary: Fetches new commits from GitHub and merges them into your local copy in one step.
entries.syntax:
cd hudm5001
git pull
entries.setup:
cd ~ && git init -q --bare course-repo.git
git clone -q course-repo.git instructor 2>/dev/null && cd instructor && echo "# HUDM 5001" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initial commit" && git push -q origin main && cd ~
git clone -q course-repo.git hudm5001-demo
cd instructor && echo "Week 2 notes" > week02.md && git add week02.md && git commit -q -m "Add week 2 notes" && git push -q origin main && cd ~
cd hudm5001-demo
entries.setup_note: your clone, made before the instructor pushed a new file
entries.output:
From /Users/student/course-repo
   903e38a..3b50d58  main       -> origin/main
Updating 903e38a..3b50d58
Fast-forward
 week02.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 week02.md
README.md
week02.md
entries.gotcha: If you edited the same lines the instructor changed, the merge stops with a conflict and git prints instructions. Commit or set aside your own edits before pulling.

entries.title: git remote — where does this repo push and pull?
entries.summary: A remote is a nickname for a repository address. `origin` is where you cloned from (your fork); `upstream` is the convention for the original repo.
entries.syntax:
git remote -v
git remote add upstream https://github.com/cgpan/hudm5001.git
entries.setup:
cd ~ && git init -q --bare my-fork.git && git init -q --bare original-repo.git
git clone -q my-fork.git hudm5001-demo 2>/dev/null && cd hudm5001-demo
entries.setup_note: a clone of your fork, with the original repo standing by
entries.example:
git remote -v
git remote add upstream ~/original-repo.git
git remote -v
entries.output:
origin	/Users/student/my-fork.git (fetch)
origin	/Users/student/my-fork.git (push)
origin	/Users/student/my-fork.git (fetch)
origin	/Users/student/my-fork.git (push)
upstream	/Users/student/original-repo.git (fetch)
upstream	/Users/student/original-repo.git (push)
entries.gotcha: Each remote is listed twice, once for fetch and once for push. Run `git remote -v` whenever you are unsure where `git push` will send your work.

entries.title: git fetch + git merge — pull from the original repo
entries.summary: The two halves of `git pull`, done by hand against the `upstream` remote: download the original repo's new commits, then merge them into your branch.
entries.syntax:
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
entries.setup:
cd ~ && git init -q --bare original-repo.git
git clone -q original-repo.git author 2>/dev/null && cd author && echo "# HUDM 5001" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Initial commit" && git push -q origin main && cd ~
git clone -q --bare original-repo.git my-fork.git
git clone -q my-fork.git hudm5001-demo
cd author && echo "Week 2 notes" > week02.md && git add week02.md && git commit -q -m "Add week 2 notes" && git push -q origin main && cd ~
cd hudm5001-demo
git remote add upstream ~/original-repo.git
entries.setup_note: your clone of your fork, after the original repo gained a commit
entries.example:
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
ls
entries.output:
From /Users/student/original-repo
 * [new branch]      main       -> upstream/main
Updating 903e38a..3b50d58
Fast-forward
 week02.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 week02.md
README.md
week02.md
entries.gotcha: `fetch` always succeeds and changes nothing in your files; only `merge` touches them. The course repo's main branch is called `main` (older projects use `master`).
